thread.title_full: Town sells $4.1M in bonds at 3% rate

author: ohtadmin
title: Town sells $4.1M in bonds at 3% rate
text:
Town Administrator Ed Mello delivered “great news” to the town council after $4.1 million in general obligation bonds were sold with a true interest cost of 3.05 percent.
The money will be used for improvements to the senior center, Town Hall, recreation center, Fort Getty, transfer station and firehouse. Eight vehicles for the department of public works and firefighting equipment also will be purchased. These projects were approved by voters in June at the financial town meeting.
Mello told the councilors at their meeting Monday about the process that begins with an analysis from Moody’s to determine the municipality’s credit rating. Jamestown’s Aa1 rating was affirmed Sept. 2 by the agency.
“It’s really good news for the community,” Mello said, “and certainly really good news for our debt service.”
The bonds were purchased Sept. 10 by Fidelity Capital Markets. Tina Collins, finance director, said they “had a great response” with only .258 percent separating the eight bids. Oppenheimer & Co. offered the highest rate at 3.30 percent. She called the 3.05 percent rate from Fidelity “very competitive in the current market.”
“Anybody would love to get that on a home mortgage today,” Mello added. “It’s actually lower than the last time we went out for bonds. It’s really remarkable.”
Mello said he “pushed a little hard” to get the highest rating, Aaa, which is the only rating higher than Aa1 from 21 levels. While that would have been “a great thing for us” because it would lead to lower interest rates, not being designated Aaa “takes the pressure off us.”
“Once you get to Aaa, you have to remain there,” Mello said.
Moody’s, in its analysis, referenced
Jamestown’s “competitive housing market,” including “the property revaluation that saw a 30 percent increase,” and said the “economy is likely to remain stable as it retains strong property values strengthened by proximity to the economies of Providence and Boston.”
“The credit quality of the town of Jamestown (Aa1) is driven by the town’s strong economy with well above-average resident income and robust full value per capita amid a largely residential tax base,” the summary reads. “The town’s credit also reflects low leverage inclusive of long-term liabilities and fixed costs ratio that are well below the medians for the sector. The town benefits from stable finances albeit with below average available reserves and liquidity that will remain consistent given small surpluses anticipated in fiscal 2025 and 2026.”
Mello said Moody’s recommended Jamestown increase its reserve to about 50 percent of its annual budget, which equates to about $15 million.
“It’s easier said than done,” he said.
The reserve is currently at 30 percent. He used this as an example of why transferring money from the reserve to offset the operating fund is not always prudent.
“Remember that when we get to budget season,” he said. “In Moody’s eyes, it’s low.”
Another challenge that keeps Jamestown from reaching Aaa is the limited commercial district. Mello, however, said this also “reduces our risk.” A city with a manufacturing plant that has thousands of employees, for example, would contribute to that economy. If that plant closed, however, it would be detrimental.
“That’s consequential to the rating for a community,” he said. “The good thing is we don’t have that risk. The bad thing is we have that to drive our rating up.”
The downside of the limited commercial district is having “all of our eggs in one basket.”
“We rely solely on residential properties in terms of our tax revenue,” he said, “and the risks that go with that.”
Moody’s was optimistic with Jamestown’s environmental, social and governance considerations.
“As an island community, the town is exposed to risks associated with sea-level rise, extreme rainfall and storms,” said the environmental analysis. “The town’s reserves and satisfactory disaster mitigation and resiliency planning adequately prepares the town to address a significant storm event. Additionally, demand for housing in the town helps to ensure strong rebuilding efforts. While over the long-term sea level rise could be a key credit risk, housing sales continue to be very strong.”
As for the other two considerations, Jamestown “has strong educational attainment, high incomes and a largely stable population” with a government that “adheres to conservative budget practices and has a long history of maintaining satisfactory reserves and liquidity.”
